analysis.one_liner: Ends the health insurance industry's exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being referred to the House Judiciary Committee and a subcommittee, it sat without a hearing or markup until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, the McCarran-Ferguson Act has shielded the insurance industry from federal antitrust laws, so health insurers could not be federally prosecuted for price fixing or other anticompetitive conduct. This bill would strip that shield for health insurance, making insurers subject to the same antitrust rules as other businesses, while also barring most consumer class-action lawsuits against insurers over antitrust violations. It was introduced with support from both parties but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and employers who buy health insurance. If insurers were subject to the same antitrust laws as other businesses, the Justice Department and FTC could prosecute price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation among insurers, and more competition could put downward pressure on premiums.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurance consumers and small employers

how_it_helps.text: Removes the industry's federal antitrust exemption so that federal laws against price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation apply to health insurers and medical malpractice insurers, the same as any other business. [S3]
Allows the FTC to police unfair methods of competition in health insurance regardless of whether the business is run for profit, closing a gap that let nonprofit insurers escape that review. [S3]
Keeps private lawsuits available for individual consumers who can show they were personally harmed by an insurer's anticompetitive conduct. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, who would lose the antitrust exemption they have held since 1945 and could face federal prosecution and civil suits for anticompetitive conduct. Some of those compliance and litigation costs could be passed to policyholders.

drawbacks.text: The bill prohibits class-action lawsuits against insurers for antitrust violations, allowing only suits by the federal or state governments or by individually named claimants. Because a single consumer's overcharge is usually too small to justify a lawsuit on its own, this would take away the main private tool consumers have had to challenge widespread anticompetitive behavior, even as the bill's own text acknowledges antitrust class actions can consume resources and affect prices. [S3]

Restoring antitrust enforcement could impose new litigation and compliance costs on insurers, and critics of removing the exemption have argued states already regulated insurers adequately, so some of the added cost could show up in premiums. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — making health insurers play by the same antitrust rules as every other business — addresses a genuine carve-out from competition law and could benefit consumers through more vigorous competition. But the bill gives with one hand and takes with the other: by banning antitrust class actions, it removes the enforcement mechanism ordinary consumers actually use, leaving primarily government agencies and well-off individual plaintiffs to police the industry. A stronger bill for consumers would have stripped the exemption without the class-action ban.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its subcommittee without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Gosar, a Republican, introduced the bill on March 17, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary. [S1] [S5]
Fourteen members cosponsored the bill, split evenly between 7 Republicans and 7 Democrats, giving it support from both parties. [S4]
On June 1, 2011, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Intellectual Property, Competition and the Internet, the last action ever taken on it. [S5]
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers came out ahead: they kept the federal antitrust exemption they have held since 1945, and no committee or floor vote was ever taken on ending it. The members who wanted the exemption lifted got nothing for their bipartisan effort.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept their antitrust exemption

for.name: Rep. Paul Gosar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end the health insurance industry's federal antitrust exemption.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or committee vote on it.

against.name: America's Health Insurance Plans and the insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Have long defended the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption and opposed congressional efforts to remove it for health insurers.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors split evenly between 7 Republicans and 7 Democrats, so the bill's inaction cannot be attributed to opposition from one party; it simply never advanced in committee.

industries.note: The bill would strip the antitrust exemption insurers have held since 1945, exposing them to federal prosecution for price fixing and market allocation. Insurers' interest in keeping that shield runs against consumers, who benefit from competitive markets.
The bill explicitly covers malpractice insurers, who would lose the same antitrust exemption and face the same antitrust exposure as other businesses.

The bill bans class actions on antitrust claims against insurers, taking away the vehicle these firms use to represent large groups of overcharged policyholders. Individual and government suits remain, but the class vehicle — often the only economically practical one for small consumer claims — is closed.
